A major winter storm impacted eastern Kentucky from January 24 through January 25, 2026, delivering a combination of heavy snow, sleet, and significant ice accretion. EVENT_NARRATIVE: A complex mix of snow, sleet, freezing rain, and rain fell across Jackson County beginning as all snow on the afternoon of the 24th and continuing for most of the 25th. A picture from just past 0900EST on the 25th showed an estimated 0.3 inches of flat ice accretion in Annville with trees starting to snap.

A major winter storm produced heavy snow and sleet across portions of northern and central Kentucky January 24-26, 2026. In addition, portions of central and eastern Kentucky saw heavy ice accumulation, which resulted in thousands of power outages. A strong low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley. The storm featured strong frontogenetical forcing in the mid-levels of the atmosphere, which led to heavy mixed precipitation and banding. A layer of warm air aloft streamed northward through central Kentucky, changing precipitation over to sleet and freezing rain for several hours. The winter storm produced damaging ice amounts of 0.25-0.80 inches in portions of central and southern Kentucky. A frigid airmass moved in following the storm, contributing to enhanced societal impact due to a combination of icy roads, power outages, and dangerously cold wind chills. Power outages across southern, central, and eastern Kentucky peaked around 75,000 on the afternoon of Sunday, January 25, 2026. The impact of this winter storm was felt for weeks following the event. A Winter Storm Warning was issued for every county in the state of Kentucky.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hart County received significant ice accumulation of 0.25 to 0.50 inches, in addition to 3 to 4 inches of snow and sleet. The wintry precipitation caused very slick and hazardous travel conditions on Interstate 65. A large truck pulling a trailer slid into and through a guardrail and went over an embankment. This crash resulted in one injury. A large SUV also slid 40 feet off Interstate 65 North, resulting in the closure of the far right lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A light wintry mix developed during the early morning hours of the 21st across portions of western Kentucky. Temperatures were highly variable across the region between 32-36 degrees, but colder ground temperatures allowed for areas of light freezing rain to develop before temperatures quickly warmed that day, resulting in slippery and icy conditions on roadways. Owensboro in Daviess County, KY experienced multiple slide offs and accidents while Marshall County, KY had ice on roadways that led to several car accidents. A single vehicle was involved in a rollover at the intersection of Moorman Cemetery Road and US 431 North in Muhlenberg County, KY, causing the northbound lanes to shut down. Slippery roads also occurred from McCracken to Henderson County, KY during the morning commute. A 57 year old female was driving a Chevy SUV north on Oaks Road near Reidland when a 42 year old female driving south in a Ford SUV hit a section of ice and spun into the northbound lane, causing an accident. Both drivers were injured, along with a 13 year old passenger. The 57 year old female did not survive her injuries after receiving treatment. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

Owensboro in Daviess County, KY experienced multiple slide offs and accidents while Marshall County, KY had ice on roadways that led to several car accidents. A single vehicle was involved in a rollover at the intersection of Moorman Cemetery Road and US 431 North in Muhlenberg County, KY, causing the northbound lanes to shut down. Slippery roads also occurred from McCracken to Henderson County, KY during the morning commute. A 57 year old female was driving a Chevy SUV north on Oaks Road near Reidland when a 42 year old female driving south in a Ford SUV hit a section of ice and spun into the northbound lane, causing an accident. Both drivers were injured, along with a 13 year old passenger. The 57 year old female did not survive her injuries after receiving treatment. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents.

A major winter storm impacted eastern Kentucky from January 24 through January 25, 2026, delivering a combination of heavy snow, sleet, and significant ice accretion. The event began with heavy snow on the afternoon of the 24th, but a potent warm nose of air aloft moved over the region overnight, transitioning precipitation into a prolonged period of freezing rain and sleet for much of the area.||The most severe icing impacts occurred in the Cumberland Basin and south-central Kentucky, where significant ice accumulations up to 0.78 inches were measured. This ice loading led to significant power outages: South Kentucky RECC reported outages peaking at over 28,000 members, while Jackson Energy peaked at 12,156 members. In many areas, the weight of the ice snapped large trees and downed power lines. Restoration efforts continued through January 31 due to the scale of the damage and hazardous terrain. As the system exited on January 26, an Arctic airmass surged into the region, causing the sloppy snow, sleet, ice to freeze into a glacier-like pack that persisted into February. This led an extended period of icy roadways. With a total liquid of 1.5 to 4.0 inches, some flooding also occurred in far southeastern Kentucky where more of the precipitation fell as rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A former CO-OP observer measured 0.25 inches of flat ice accretion in Island City at 1825EST on the 25th. The icing followed a period of mixed precipitation, leading to slick roads and drooping trees.

A strong upper-level trough and an intensifying coastal low off the Eastern Seaboard combined to produce a fluffy snowfall event across southeastern Kentucky from January 30th through January 31st, 2026. The system was characterized by a persistent west-to-east oriented frontogenetic snow band that developed south of the Mountain Parkway. As the coastal system intensified into a powerful Nor'easter, the band pivoted and became nearly stationary along the Kentucky-Virginia border, leading to an extended period of light to moderate snowfall.||The highest accumulations were concentrated in the high terrain of Pike, Letcher, and Harlan counties, where totals reached 4.0 to 5.0 inches. Because of the extremely cold Arctic airmass in place, snow-to-liquid ratios were high, ranging from 14:1 to 19:1, resulting in a very dry, powdery snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall was widespread across the county. A CO-OP observer at Lilley Cornett Woods (Skyline) measured 4.0 inches of snow at 0803EST on the 31st. Additionally, a CoCoRaHS observer at Mayking 1.4 ENE reported a storm total of 3.7 inches of dry, powdery snow.

A prolonged period of wintry weather impacted eastern Kentucky from February 22 into February 24, 2026, as a deep upper-level trough over the eastern United States funneled a moist, modified polar airmass into the region. This setup established a persistent northwesterly upslope flow regime, resulting in scattered to numerous snow showers. These showers were frequently cellular in nature and produced squall-like conditions at some locations.||Accumulations varied significantly across the region due to the convective and orographic nature of the event. While many locations near and west of Pottsville Escarpment saw only a dusting to an inch, higher terrain in the southeast experienced much more substantial totals. The heaviest totals were generally concentrated near the Pine and Black Mountains in the far east, where persistent upslope forcing maximized snowfall. However, isolated similarly heavy swaths were also noted upstream of these higher mountains over portions of Lee and Owsley counties, where convective snow bands persisted for extended periods. Despite high snow-to-liquid ratios of 15:1 to 40:1 for most locations, leading to dry, fluffy snow, the intensity of the showers caused slick and hazardous travel conditions on untreated roads.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant convective snowfall was noted upstream of the higher terrain. A CoCoRaHS observer located 3.6 miles east-northeast of Booneville measured a storm total of 4.1 inches of snow by the morning of the 24th.

As the system's cold front crossed the region overnight, the threat transitioned to isolated damaging winds. High-momentum air mixing to the surface downed trees and utility lines in Lee and Breathitt counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The local highway department reported that a tree had been blown down onto powerlines between MM10 and MM12 along KY-1812.

A cold air mass with sub-freezing temperatures that originated from Siberia was reinforced by a major winter storm that brought a snowpack across portions of western Kentucky on the 25th. Breezy west to northwest winds with occasional gusts around 20 mph caused dangerous intervals of wind chills between -10 to locally -18 in Union and Henderson County, KY on the 26th. Far southeast portions of the Kentucky Pennyrile only experienced advisory criteria with wind chills around -8. Meanwhile, wind chills across portions of the Kentucky Purchase continued to remain below advisory criteria of 0 since the night of the 23rd. Dangerous wind chills eventually came to an end during the morning hours of the 27th. The one exception was in Carlisle, Ballard, and McCracken County, KY where wind chills warmed above -5 during the late morning hours of the 26th due to calmer winds.

A strong cold front moved across western Kentucky, followed by a ridge of high pressure that originated from Siberia, bringing prolonged sub-freezing temperatures beginning on the 23rd. Breezy northerly winds with gusts over 20 mph caused wind chills to plummet between -1 to -9 degrees during the evening hours and continued into the morning of the 24th. Southwest portions of the Kentucky Purchase region experienced another interval of dangerous wind chills on the 25th while the Kentucky Pennyrile region remained warmer above advisory criteria when a major winter storm was ongoing.

A major winter storm produced heavy snow and sleet across portions of northern and central Kentucky January 24-26, 2026. In addition, portions of central and eastern Kentucky saw heavy ice accumulation, which resulted in thousands of power outages. A strong low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley. The storm featured strong frontogenetical forcing in the mid-levels of the atmosphere, which led to heavy mixed precipitation and banding. A layer of warm air aloft streamed northward through central Kentucky, changing precipitation over to sleet and freezing rain for several hours. The winter storm produced damaging ice amounts of 0.25-0.80 inches in portions of central and southern Kentucky. A frigid airmass moved in following the storm, contributing to enhanced societal impact due to a combination of icy roads, power outages, and dangerously cold wind chills. Power outages across southern, central, and eastern Kentucky peaked around 75,000 on the afternoon of Sunday, January 25, 2026. The impact of this winter storm was felt for weeks following the event. A Winter Storm Warning was issued for every county in the state of Kentucky.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Bullitt County received 5 to 6 inches of heavy snow and sleet. Bullitt County also received light ice accumulation. The winter storm produced very dangerous travel conditions, and a semi truck was involved in a rollover crash on Interstate 65.

Precipitation lingered overnight then tapered off the morning of the 26th.||Ice amounts ranged from three-tenths to half an inch in northeast Kentucky. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm that brought Paducah's 7th largest snowstorm on record impacted western Kentucky on the 24th with light to moderate snow developing during the morning hours. After a brief lull in the evening, moderate to heavy sleet developed with a second wave that continued overnight into the morning hours of the 25th as above freezing temperatures aloft advected north. The warm layer was deep enough across far southern Kentucky into part of the Pennyrile that allowed for a period of freezing rain to occur. Colder air wrapped around on the backside, allowing for precipitation to transition back to all snow before ending during the afternoon hours. Between 4 to 8 inches of snow and sleet was observed. Ice amounts were generally a glaze to a tenth of an inch, but localized amounts in Muhlenberg, Todd, and Christian County, KY were near 1/4 inch of ice accretion. ||Significant travel impacts were experienced with snow instantly accumulating on all surfaces due to temperatures only in the upper single digits and teens during the bulk of the event. Roads became impassible closer to the Ohio River where 1 to 2 inches of sleet led to a very dense accumulation on road surfaces and the worst driving conditions in 15 to 20 years in McCracken County, KY. Between exit 7 and 4 westbound on Interstate 24, a semi-truck slid off the highway near Paducah. The weight from the sleet also caused a carport collapse in West Paducah. The Sheriff's Office in Lyon County, KY posted multiple requests to limit travel to emergency and essential situations only after responding to stranded motorists and observing abandoned vehicles in several locations. Multiple four-wheel drive vehicles even became stuck in the snow and sleet. Due to the very dangerous travel conditions, even first responders got stuck during the early morning hours of the 25th while a plow truck was also trapped in a ditch while trying to clear roads of ice and snow. Across Daviess County, KY, emergency crews responded to 10 calls for non-injury accidents with law enforcement providing assistance to 88 motorists that included drivers stuck in the snow. An 84 year old man and sports hall of famer had passed away at his son's home in Livingston County, KY near Salem the Wednesday following the storm after experiencing a medical emergency. The man walked a short distance to his home after his vehicle became stuck in the snow on the 28th. The greatest power outages were confined to mainly Todd County, KY where 10-15% customers were without power due to an ice storm clipping the area locally. The HPX WSR-88D radar at Fort Campbell in Christian County, KY had 2 inches of ice accumulated on the antenna that made it difficult for technicians to reestablish communications for several days. The City of Paducah, McCracken County, and the entire commonwealth of Kentucky, all declared a State of Emergency prior to the storm. Wind gusts around 20 to 25 mph led to blowing and drifting snow before the transition to a wintry mix. The extreme cold after the event hampered clean-up efforts and made snow and ice removal extremely difficult. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, road closures, government closures, scattered power outages.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged period of wintry weather impacted eastern Kentucky from February 22 into February 24, 2026, as a deep upper-level trough over the eastern United States funneled a moist, modified polar airmass into the region. This setup established a persistent northwesterly upslope flow regime, resulting in scattered to numerous snow showers. These showers were frequently cellular in nature and produced squall-like conditions at some locations.||Accumulations varied significantly across the region due to the convective and orographic nature of the event. While many locations near and west of Pottsville Escarpment saw only a dusting to an inch, higher terrain in the southeast experienced much more substantial totals. The heaviest totals were generally concentrated near the Pine and Black Mountains in the far east, where persistent upslope forcing maximized snowfall. However, isolated similarly heavy swaths were also noted upstream of these higher mountains over portions of Lee and Owsley counties, where convective snow bands persisted for extended periods. Despite high snow-to-liquid ratios of 15:1 to 40:1 for most locations, leading to dry, fluffy snow, the intensity of the showers caused slick and hazardous travel conditions on untreated roads.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Orographic enhancement resulted in significant totals along the high ridges. KYTC estimated 6.0 inches of snow on top of Pine Mountain along both US-119 (Oven Fork) and along US-23 at the Virginia state line (2,360 feet elevation). The Mayking 1.4 ENE Cocorahs station measured 3.1 inches, while a CO-OP observer in Skyline measured 1.5 inches. Only 1.5 inches was estimated by the local highway garage in the valleys near Colly.

A major winter storm produced heavy snow and sleet across portions of northern and central Kentucky January 24-26, 2026. In addition, portions of central and eastern Kentucky saw heavy ice accumulation, which resulted in thousands of power outages. A strong low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley. The storm featured strong frontogenetical forcing in the mid-levels of the atmosphere, which led to heavy mixed precipitation and banding. A layer of warm air aloft streamed northward through central Kentucky, changing precipitation over to sleet and freezing rain for several hours. The winter storm produced damaging ice amounts of 0.25-0.80 inches in portions of central and southern Kentucky. A frigid airmass moved in following the storm, contributing to enhanced societal impact due to a combination of icy roads, power outages, and dangerously cold wind chills. Power outages across southern, central, and eastern Kentucky peaked around 75,000 on the afternoon of Sunday, January 25, 2026. The impact of this winter storm was felt for weeks following the event. A Winter Storm Warning was issued for every county in the state of Kentucky.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Allen County received damaging ice accumulation of 0.50-0.65 inches. This ice accumulation caused tree and power line damage, which resulted in thousands without power. Snow and sleet accumulation of around 3 inches also impacted the county.

A significant winter storm brought a mix of wintry precipitation to the area from the afternoon of January 24th into the 26th. Precipitation initially overspread the area as snow the evening of the 24th, then transitioned to a mix of snow, sleet, and freezing rain overnight into the morning of the 25th. Portions of northeast KY, southwest VA, and central and southern WV also experienced a period of rain as temperatures warmed slightly during the day. Temperatures plunged back below freezing in the wake of a cold front, with precipitation turning back to snow throughout the area that evening. Precipitation lingered overnight then tapered off the morning of the 26th.||Ice amounts ranged from three-tenths to half an inch in northeast Kentucky. In addition to ice, two to three inches of snow fell across the area. Ice accumulations led to power outages and downed some trees near the communities of Flatwoods, Raceland, and Yatesville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm that brought Paducah's 7th largest snowstorm on record impacted western Kentucky on the 24th with light to moderate snow developing during the morning hours. After a brief lull in the evening, moderate to heavy sleet developed with a second wave that continued overnight into the morning hours of the 25th as above freezing temperatures aloft advected north. The warm layer was deep enough across far southern Kentucky into part of the Pennyrile that allowed for a period of freezing rain to occur. Colder air wrapped around on the backside, allowing for precipitation to transition back to all snow before ending during the afternoon hours. Between 4 to 8 inches of snow and sleet was observed. Ice amounts were generally a glaze to a tenth of an inch, but localized amounts in Muhlenberg, Todd, and Christian County, KY were near 1/4 inch of ice accretion. ||Significant travel impacts were experienced with snow instantly accumulating on all surfaces due to temperatures only in the upper single digits and teens during the bulk of the event. Roads became impassible closer to the Ohio River where 1 to 2 inches of sleet led to a very dense accumulation on road surfaces and the worst driving conditions in 15 to 20 years in McCracken County, KY. Between exit 7 and 4 westbound on Interstate 24, a semi-truck slid off the highway near Paducah. The weight from the sleet also caused a carport collapse in West Paducah. The Sheriff's Office in Lyon County, KY posted multiple requests to limit travel to emergency and essential situations only after responding to stranded motorists and observing abandoned vehicles in several locations. Multiple four-wheel drive vehicles even became stuck in the snow and sleet. Due to the very dangerous travel conditions, even first responders got stuck during the early morning hours of the 25th while a plow truck was also trapped in a ditch while trying to clear roads of ice and snow. Across Daviess County, KY, emergency crews responded to 10 calls for non-injury accidents with law enforcement providing assistance to 88 motorists that included drivers stuck in the snow. An 84 year old man and sports hall of famer had passed away at his son's home in Livingston County, KY near Salem the Wednesday following the storm after experiencing a medical emergency. The man walked a short distance to his home after his vehicle became stuck in the snow on the 28th. The greatest power outages were confined to mainly Todd County, KY where 10-15% customers were without power due to an ice storm clipping the area locally. The HPX WSR-88D radar at Fort Campbell in Christian County, KY had 2 inches of ice accumulated on the antenna that made it difficult for technicians to reestablish communications for several days. The City of Paducah, McCracken County, and the entire commonwealth of Kentucky, all declared a State of Emergency prior to the storm. Wind gusts around 20 to 25 mph led to blowing and drifting snow before the transition to a wintry mix. The extreme cold after the event hampered clean-up efforts and made snow and ice removal extremely difficult. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, road closures, government closures, scattered power outages.

A cold air mass with sub-freezing temperatures that originated from Siberia was reinforced by a major winter storm that brought a snowpack across portions of western Kentucky on the 25th. Breezy west to northwest winds with occasional gusts around 20 mph caused dangerous intervals of wind chills between -10 to locally -18 in Union and Henderson County, KY on the 26th. Far southeast portions of the Kentucky Pennyrile only experienced advisory criteria with wind chills around -8. Meanwhile, wind chills across portions of the Kentucky Purchase continued to remain below advisory criteria of 0 since the night of the 23rd. Dangerous wind chills eventually came to an end during the morning hours of the 27th. The one exception was in Carlisle, Ballard, and McCracken County, KY where wind chills warmed above -5 during the late morning hours of the 26th due to calmer winds.

A major winter storm produced heavy snow and sleet across portions of northern and central Kentucky January 24-26, 2026. In addition, portions of central and eastern Kentucky saw heavy ice accumulation, which resulted in thousands of power outages. A strong low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley. The storm featured strong frontogenetical forcing in the mid-levels of the atmosphere, which led to heavy mixed precipitation and banding. A layer of warm air aloft streamed northward through central Kentucky, changing precipitation over to sleet and freezing rain for several hours. The winter storm produced damaging ice amounts of 0.25-0.80 inches in portions of central and southern Kentucky. A frigid airmass moved in following the storm, contributing to enhanced societal impact due to a combination of icy roads, power outages, and dangerously cold wind chills. Power outages across southern, central, and eastern Kentucky peaked around 75,000 on the afternoon of Sunday, January 25, 2026. The impact of this winter storm was felt for weeks following the event. A Winter Storm Warning was issued for every county in the state of Kentucky.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Meade County received 5 to 6 inches of heavy snow and sleet, in addition to light ice accumulation around 0.10 inches.

A surface low in the Central Plains moved northeast into the Great Lakes late on Sunday the 15th. Ahead of its attendant cold front that passed later in the evening, a low level jet developed in the late morning and moved east. Daytime heating gave added energy to mix the lower levels of the atmosphere and bring strong winds from this feature to the surface.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The ASOS at the Cincinnati Airport (KCVG) measured a gust to 49 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and early evening hours on May 16th, a Mesoscale Convective Vortex moved from west-southwest to east-northeast across the lower Ohio Valley, providing forcing for scattered showers and thunderstorms to develop. Thunderstorms were able to feed off of a seasonably high amount of instability, with around 2000 J/kg Mixed-Layer CAPE present in the pre-storm environment. While synoptic scale ridging over the southeast US meant that large scale flow was fairly weak, the MCV provided a mesoscale enhancement to the wind shear profile, with around 30-35 knots of effective shear supporting organized multicell clusters. Scattered strong to severe storms moved along the Ohio River in north central Kentucky, producing several reports of wind damage as well as isolated instances of near-severe sized hail. The most robust storm of the evening produced a 65 mph wind gust as it moved across Oldham and Henry County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized hail was observed in downtown Louisville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On May 18th into May 19th, the Ohio Valley was in the middle of a southwest mid- and upper-level flow regime between troughing over the central CONUS and southeast US ridging. Smaller scale perturbations within the broader flow pattern would support a couple waves of showers and thunderstorms, with isolated strong to severe storms occurring across north central Kentucky and southern Indiana during the afternoon and evening hours both days. These stronger cells were able to produce a few instances of wind damage vai downed trees as well as near-severe level hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A unique event with limited severe weather and flash flooding occurred during the evening hours on May 22nd. A surface low pressure system slowly moved across western Kentucky, with a warm front extending to the east-northeast across much of Kentucky. Along and south of this warm front, precipitable water values exceeding 1.7 inches lead to showers and a few thunderstorms which produced efficient rainfall rates. Where heavier showers and storms trained over eastern Shelby, Henry, and western Franklin County, a few instances of flash flooding were observed. Closer to the surface low pressure center, marginal amounts of instability (around 250-500 J/kg MLCAPE) combined with relatively impressive amounts of low-level shear and helicity along the warm front to produce miniature supercells. One of these mini supercells produced a brief EF0 tornado in Butler County near Butler County High School.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Bardstown Trail was closed due to water flowing over the roadway.

On May 18th into May 19th, the Ohio Valley was in the middle of a southwest mid- and upper-level flow regime between troughing over the central CONUS and southeast US ridging. Smaller scale perturbations within the broader flow pattern would support a couple waves of showers and thunderstorms, with isolated strong to severe storms occurring across north central Kentucky and southern Indiana during the afternoon and evening hours both days. While effective bulk shear was relatively unsupportive of organized convection around 20 knots, a few stronger cores were able to develop thanks to 2000-2500 J/kg of mixed-layer CAPE. These stronger cells were able to produce a few instances of wind damage vai downed trees as well as near-severe level hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail was reported along Herbert Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. While the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, resulting in a quasi-linear convective system, some scattered cells developed ahead of the main line of storms across western Kentucky. These storms had transient supercellular characteristics, and would go on to produce a swath of stronger winds and a few embedded tornadoes across Butler, Grayson, Breckinridge, Hardin, and Meade County. Elsewhere across Kentucky, scattered wind damage was produced by the main line of storms, with more favorably oriented segments of the line producing additional weak spin-up tornadoes. As the line of storms pushed east toward the I-75 corridor early in the morning on March 16th, there was a general weakening trend as MLCAPE values dropped to only around 100 J/kg across the Bluegrass. However, the portion of the line across southern Kentucky had access to slightly greater instability, resulting in additional instances of wind damage and a spin-up tornado in Clinton County. The line of storms eventually pushed into eastern Kentucky by around 3 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the region behind the cold front.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful storm system caused a rapid transition from record-nearing warmth to winter conditions across eastern Kentucky on March 16th. The event began as a cold front and associated squall line crossed the region between midnight and 6:00 AM EST, producing a peak measured wind gust of 62 mph at the Somerset-Pulaski County Airport (KSME) and widespread strong gusts over 40 mph elsewhere. These winds downed numerous trees and power lines, resulting in localized power outages and blocked roads, especially in Wayne, Rockcastle, and Pulaski counties.||Following the frontal passage, temperatures fell dramatically, plummeting more than 40 degrees from the 70s into the 30s. After a mid-morning lull in precipitation, a secondary wave of low pressure riding along the departing cold front brought steady stratiform snow by midday. During the afternoon and evening, this evolved into a convective regime as steep low-level lapse rates fueled snow showers and squalls. With high snow-to-liquid ratios, accumulations reached to around 4 inches in the high terrain of Pike, Letcher, and Floyd counties, while moderate totals of 1 to 3 inches were noted most other places east of I-75 and southeast of I-64. The snow showers tapered to flurries by early March 17th as temperatures settled in the 20s.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Leslie County dispatch reported a tree blown down in the MM 3 to 4 stretch of KY-699 in the vicinity of Smilax.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. While the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, resulting in a quasi-linear convective system, some scattered cells developed ahead of the main line of storms across western Kentucky. These storms had transient supercellular characteristics, and would go on to produce a swath of stronger winds and a few embedded tornadoes across Butler, Grayson, Breckinridge, Hardin, and Meade County. Elsewhere across Kentucky, scattered wind damage was produced by the main line of storms, with more favorably oriented segments of the line producing additional weak spin-up tornadoes. As the line of storms pushed east toward the I-75 corridor early in the morning on March 16th, there was a general weakening trend as MLCAPE values dropped to only around 100 J/kg across the Bluegrass. However, the portion of the line across southern Kentucky had access to slightly greater instability, resulting in additional instances of wind damage and a spin-up tornado in Clinton County. The line of storms eventually pushed into eastern Kentucky by around 3 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the region behind the cold front.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms swept through northeast Kentucky during the predawn hours of March 16th in response to a passing cold front. Downed trees and power lines were observed in Boyd and Lawrence Counties as a result of these stronger storms. Outside of thunderstorms, a period of strong synoptic winds accompanying this disturbance took place. Surface winds picked up in intensity in the wake of the storms and remained elevated into the morning hours of the 16th. The strongest observation of these winds in northeast Kentucky were noted shortly after the round of storms swept through between 4 and 4:30 AM, where Mesonet stations and the AWOS in Ashland recorded winds ranging from 35 to 42 miles per hour. As high pressure built in from the west on the 16th, gradient winds diminished.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system pressing through the Great Lakes region on March 13th resulted in a windy day across northeast Kentucky. This was due to the combination of a tightened pressure gradient and strengthening low level jet aloft. Daytime heating helped to create turbulent mixing of these stronger winds down to the surface, especially during the afternoon and early evening hours. Wind gusts in excess of 40 to 50 miles per hour noted in northeast Kentucky resulted in downed trees and power lines across the area. The wind gradually declined after sunset that evening as the pressure gradient eased its hold over the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. Elsewhere across Kentucky, scattered wind damage was produced by the main line of storms, with more favorably oriented segments of the line producing additional weak spin-up tornadoes. As the line of storms pushed east toward the I-75 corridor early in the morning on March 16th, there was a general weakening trend as MLCAPE values dropped to only around 100 J/kg across the Bluegrass. However, the portion of the line across southern Kentucky had access to slightly greater instability, resulting in additional instances of wind damage and a spin-up tornado in Clinton County. The line of storms eventually pushed into eastern Kentucky by around 3 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the region behind the cold front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Radar data indicated a large area of strong inbound velocity along a path east of the couplet that caused the third tornado along that storm's path. High resolution satellite imagery indicated a large incoherent patch of trees damaged just west of Salt River Rd south of Berrytown Rd. Additional trees were noted on ground survey damage along Salt River Rd just south of New Salem Church Rd. Another barn and silo were damaged near the intersection of Berrytown Rd and DeWitt Ln. Damage continued upstream along Rineyville Rd where a larger outdoor garage had its roof peeled off before the tornado entered into Meade County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The west Kentucky climate division experienced their driest Nov-Mar on record with only 9.61, which was 11.32 below normal, leaving much of west Kentucky in Moderate (D1) Drought at the very end of March. This included the northern Jackson Purchase area, the Lakes region, and the Pennyrile. A very warm April, with temperatures running 7-8 degrees F above normal, along with April precipitation 1-2in. below normal, and especially a soil moisture ranking near the 1st percentile, resulted in intensification of drought through April. At the end of April, most of west Kentucky was in Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought with drought continuing into May. Agricultural impacts primarily took the form of earlier than normal planting and very low farm pond levels. Subsoil and topsoil conditions remained quite poor.

The west Kentucky climate division experienced their driest Nov-Mar on record with only 9.61, which was 11.32 below normal, leaving much of west Kentucky in Moderate (D1) Drought at the very end of March. This included the northern Jackson Purchase area, the Lakes region, and the Pennyrile. A very warm April, with temperatures running 7-8 degrees F above normal, along with April precipitation 1-2in. below normal, and especially a soil moisture ranking near the 1st percentile, resulted in intensification of drought through April. At the end of April, most of west Kentucky was in Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought with drought continuing into May. Agricultural impacts primarily took the form of earlier than normal planting and very low farm pond levels. Subsoil and topsoil conditions remained quite poor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With low pressure strengthening and tracking northeastward towards Chicago, the Quad State region experienced breezy southerly to southeasterly winds throughout the daytime hours. Spotty wind gusts to 40+mph were observed in West Kentucky, with the strongest gust measured 46mph at the Sturgis Municipal Airport's AWOS site. Showers and a few thunderstorms moved eastward across West Kentucky during the late afternoon to early evening hours.

Multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted the Quad State region on the 27th. The later rounds of storms began with isolated to scattered storms tracking northeastward late afternoon into the early evening. On the synoptic scale, an upper level jet ejected across the Missouri Valley during the evening with a pronounced mid level wave moving through. The low level jet strengthened into the evening. A surface low was positioned near St Louis during the early evening with a trailing cold front extending southwestward. A broken band of supercells developed along this and eventually congealed into more linear segments as it moved into Southern Illinois and West Kentucky compared to its more discrete structure in Southeast Missouri.||In Northwest Kentucky, during the late evening, MLCAPE remained elevated ahead of the frontal boundary with values of 1000-2000J/kg, along with deep layer shear of 50-60kts, STP of 4-6, and mid-level lapse rates of 8C.||Reports from West Kentucky primarily came from an intensifying line of storms entering the Western Coal Fields area from the northwest. The most significant damage came from a surging portion of the line with an embedded supercell that resulted in two tornadoes: 1. an EF-0 tornado which crossed from northeastern Hopkins County into McLean County, and 2. an EF-1 tornado which caused damage from southeast of Rumsey to north of Livermore in McLean County. A swath of straight-line winds accompanied the first tornadic circulation. The tornadoes damaged numerous trees, some electrical lines and power poles, and a few homes and outbuildings. Several other straight-line wind damage reports were received.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree damage was reported north of Livermore on US-431 between Atherton and KY-1080. This damage is north of the surveyed tornado track.

The west Kentucky climate division experienced their driest Nov-Mar on record with only 9.61, which was 11.32 below normal, leaving much of west Kentucky in Moderate (D1) Drought at the very end of March. This included the northern Jackson Purchase area, the Lakes region, and the Pennyrile. A very warm April, with temperatures running 7-8 degrees F above normal, along with April precipitation 1-2in. below normal, and especially a soil moisture ranking near the 1st percentile, resulted in intensification of drought through April. At the end of April, most of west Kentucky was in Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) Drought with drought continuing into May. Agricultural impacts primarily took the form of earlier than normal planting and very low farm pond levels. Subsoil and topsoil conditions remained quite poor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of storms occurred June 26-28th, 2026 resulting in significant flash flooding over southern Indiana and central Kentucky as well as an EF-0 tornado.  Several flash flood warnings were issued over the 2 day period with Considerable Flash Flooding in multiple locations and even Flash Flood Emergencies in some areas. Rainfall totals for the weekend ended up in an area wide 2-4 inches with swaths of 6-10+ inches!!  Unfortunately 3 fatalities were confirmed due to flooding in Madison County, KY, and 1 fatality indirectly related to the flooding occurred on Floyds Fork in Jefferson County, KY.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two people were trapped and drowned in a basement apartment on the 300 block of University Drive after the outside entrance, 10 feet below ground level, filled with water.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The National Weather Service conducted a storm survey in Meade County, Kentucky for the storms that moved through the region late Sunday night, June 21, 2026.  The nature of the damage was consistent with straight line wind damage between 80 and 85 mph in the Big Bend area of Meade county.||Damage was first observed on Big Bend Road where several trees were uprooted or snapped due to the high winds.  Paradise Bottom Road also had some tree damage.  Damaged areas north of the rock quarry near Big Bend Road had a similar direction facing to the north.  Tree damage continued along Battletown Road north of Battletown.  All damage south of the rock quarry near Big Bend Road was facing to the south. These damage directions would indicate a thunderstorm downburst likely occurred in the Big Bend area with winds spreading out in different divergent directions, evident of a thunderstorm downburst.
